item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","answer":"SCOPe places these catalytic domains in the protein kinase-like fold (d.144) and protein kinase-like superfamily (d.144.1). Their shared bilobal architecture, nucleotide-binding cleft, and corresponding catalytic/metal-binding features support a homologous catalytic core and a broadly conserved ATP-dependent phosphoryl-transfer mechanism. This does not make them functionally interchangeable: canonical protein kinases phosphorylate protein residues, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases phosphorylate antibiotic substrates, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases phosphorylate membrane phosphoinositides. Superfamily membership supports remote common ancestry, but not close family-level homology, identical substrate recognition, or conserved regulation. Substrate specificity requires external evidence such as sequence/profile analysis of specificity determinants, active-site structural comparison (preferably with nucleotide and substrate or analog bound), biochemical substrate-panel assays and kinetics, and ideally mutational validation. Regulatory transfer additionally requires evidence for matching domain architecture, regulatory motifs and phosphorylation sites, interaction partners, localization or membrane-recruitment context, and direct cellular or biochemical regulation assays. A representative from another family may be a useful catalytic-fold or active-site template, but it is unsafe as a substrate-bound, regulatory, or full-length functional template without those validations; representatives should be selected at the closest supported family/sequence level and in the relevant conformational and ligand state.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
